one_liner: Parallel, block-indexed xz compressor CLI; roughly ties multi-threaded xz on speed, adds random access into .tpxz tarballs.
what_it_does: A command-line replacement for xz that splits input into independent LZMA2 blocks, compresses and decompresses them on all cores, and writes a standard .xz stream. When the input is a tarball it also stores a file index (member name and offset) as an extra block, so 'pixz -l' lists members and 'pixz -x path' extracts one member without decompressing the whole archive. It works as 'tar -Ipixz', but its flags differ from xz (-t, -l, -f, -q mean other things; no -z, -c is ignored) and it has no library API.
how_it_is_fast: A pthread pipeline: one reader thread cuts input into blocks of 2x the LZMA2 dictionary size (16 MiB at -6, 128 MiB at -9; tunable with -f), N worker threads run liblzma's block encoder or decoder on separate blocks, and the main thread writes them back in sequence order. Because every block header carries its sizes and the xz index lists them, decompression can also be split across threads, and the tar file index lets extraction seek straight to the needed blocks. The compression itself is plain liblzma at the chosen preset, so per-core speed is xz's.
when_to_use: Large tarballs (backups, datasets, build artifacts) that must stay in .xz format but where you later need to list members or pull out single files quickly
Systems with XZ Utils older than 5.4, which cannot decompress with multiple threads, or older than 5.6, where xz is single-threaded unless given -T
Pipelines that already use 'tar -I' and want multi-core LZMA2 at xz's ratio without changing the archive format readers expect
Multi-gigabyte single files where parallel decompression of an .xz you produce yourself matters
when_not_to_use: You already run XZ Utils 5.4+ with -T: in the only third-party run found (pRDS, 3 GB tweet CSV, 4-core i7 Mac) pixz -6 was 443 s versus 469 s for xz -T at equal threads, with 1.3% larger output, a gap one informal run cannot separate from noise

You need byte-exact round trips through plain 'xz -d' of tar input: in tar mode the file index is written as an extra LZMA2 block inside the same stream, so xz -d emits it as trailing bytes (consistent with open issue #65, where 'pixz -0 | xz -d' produced 3.9 MB more than the 4.38 GB input); use -t
Speed matters more than the .xz format: catalogued siblings such as bzip3, libbsc, Kanzi or lrzip compress several times faster than xz in their own runs
Memory-constrained hosts: about ceil(1.3N+1) blocks are in flight plus one LZMA2 coder per thread, and the out-of-memory issue #44 and 'Error creating block encoder' #97 are open

You need an actively released tool: the last release is 1.0.7 (2020-07-26); later commits (to 2025-03-08) are unreleased and 33 issues are open, including an unresolved decompression deadlock (#35) and a 'stream footer' failure on a 3.1 TiB file (#102)

integration.form: command-line program (autotools build); no library API
integration.dependencies: liblzma 4.999.9beta-212 or later, libarchive 2.8 or later, pthreads, libm; AsciiDoc only for the man page (can be built without since 1.0.7)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (AC_PROG_CC_STDC), autoconf 2.68+ and pkg-config when building from git
integration.platforms: Linux (glibc and musl), macOS, BSD-style endian headers handled; Windows build fixes (seekability, CPU count) are in unreleased 2023 commits
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (standalone process); internally one reader, N coder threads (all cores via sched_getaffinity or sysconf, cap with -p) and one writer
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: output is a valid .xz stream that xz can decompress and 'tar -Ipixz' works, but CLI flags and default file naming differ from xz and tar-mode output carries an extra index block

gotchas: Source finding: when given an input file and an output path, src/pixz.c opens the output with open(opath, O_CREAT | O_WRONLY, mode) and no O_TRUNC (no ftruncate anywhere), so writing over an existing longer file leaves its old tail after the new data: a corrupt .xz on compression, silently extra bytes on 'pixz -d in.xz out' decompression. Shell redirection and stdin input (fopen 'w') are not affected; delete the target first.

Tar detection is automatic and changes the payload: in tar mode an index block is appended and pixz -d verifies and filters it with a heuristic ('File index heuristic failed, use -t flag'); open issue #80 asks to document that payloads may be modified. Use -t for non-tar data.

The README's two speed arguments are dated: xz 5.4.0 (2022-12-13) added a threaded decompressor for multi-block files with sizes in block headers, and xz 5.6.0 NEWS lists multithreaded mode as the default, so the remaining distinctive feature is the tarball index.

Parallel decompression only helps on multi-block files: an .xz written by single-threaded xz is one block and decodes on one core; issue #71 reports idle cores during decompression of a 13 GB file on a 16-thread Ryzen.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick pixz when you must emit .xz and want random access to tarball members; for raw speed in the LZMA2 family Fast LZMA2 reports 20-100% faster encoding than 7-Zip's LZMA2 at high levels, and if the format is free, bzip3, libbsc, Kanzi or lrzip beat xz outright in their catalogued runs, while pigz is the analogous tool for gzip.
verified_claims_summary: The only measurement is one informal third-party run in the pRDS R package's README (2020): writing and reading an R object of about 17 million tweets (3 GB CSV) on a 4-core/8-thread i7 Mac, pixz -tp<cores> -6 took 443 s to write and 63 s to read versus 469 s and 64 s for xz -zcT<cores> -6 at the same thread count, about 1.06x faster compression with 805 MB versus 795 MB output; reads go through R's deserializer from a pipe, so the read rows are R-bound, and no tool versions or repeats are given.
status_note: Stale but not abandoned: last release 1.0.7 in 2020, sporadic unreleased commits through 2025-03-08, 33 open issues; BSD-2-Clause and packaged by distributions (Fedora and openSUSE packages appear in search results), so usable as a CLI, but treat it as an indexing tool rather than a speed upgrade over modern xz -T.
